المعادلة تغيرت تماماً اليوم؛ فالتقديس #التقليدي للماركات الأوروبية بدأ يتآكل أمام واقع تكنولوجي واقتصادي جديد فرضته الصين، والتي نجحت في كشف زيف الأسعار الفلكية التي تدفعها مقابل "الاسم والإرث" فقط. شركات صينية رائدة مثل #BYD و #Zeekr وLi #Auto أثبتت أن الفخامة الحقيقية تكمن في الابتكار، من خلال تقديم #سيارات كهربائية وهجينة تمثل "كمبيوترات ذكية على عجلات" متفوقة برمجياً وبطاريات من الجيل الجديد ومنصات شحن فائقة السرعة، وبنصف تكلفة نظيراتها #الأوروبية. هذا التفوق الصيني، المدعوم بالسيطرة الكاملة على سلاسل إمداد البطاريات والتكامل العمودي، لم يترك للشركات الأوروبية العريقة خياراً سوى الهروب نحو فرض جمارك وضرائب حمائية، بعد أن عجزت عن مجاراة الصين في تقديم مواصفات ثورية بأسعار عادلة تناسب المستهلك الذكي.

معليش على الاطالة بس كان ودي اعرف ادق التفاصيل الفنية بخصوص هذي السيارة اللي اختلفوا فيها ولا احد قادر يجيب العلم الاكيد.

هل السيارة صناعة صينية بالكامل حتى المكينة تصنع في شانجان فورد؟ 
-  نعم، السيارة تُصنّع بالكامل داخل الصين – الهيكل والمكينة والقير كلها تُنتج محلياً عن طريق المشروع المشترك، مو قطع أمريكية تتجمّع في الصين. حتى المكاين (عائلة الإيكوبوست) تُصنّع في مصنع محرّكات تشانجان فورد داخل الصين. لكن لاحظ الفرق المهم: "تُصنع في الصين" لا يعني "تصميم/هندسة صينية" – الأساس الهندسي فورد.

هل فيه من سيارات شانجان من تشترك مع التورس بأي شيء؟
- لا، تشانجان فورد مشروع مشترك ينتج سيارات بماركة فورد فقط للسوق الصيني، وما فيه سيارات بماركة شانجان تتباع تحت فورد ولا العكس. سيارات شانجان الخاصة (UNI-T, UNI-K, Eado…) تمشي على منصّات ومكاين شانجان (Blue Whale) ومالها أي علاقة بمنصة أو مكينة التورس.


إشراف فورد بس، ولا صناعة مشتركة بين الشركتين؟
- صناعة مشتركة فعلياً، مو مجرد إشراف. تشانجان فورد شركة مناصفة 50/50 بين فورد موتور وشركة تشانجان الصينية (مدعومة من الدولة)، تأسست 2001. فورد توفّر الهيكلة والهندسة الأساسية للسيارة، والقرارات الاستراتيجية تتطلب موافقة الطرفين. يعني العضم الهندسي فورد، والتصنيع والتوطين والتكيّف للسوق الصيني تشانجان.


فيها قطع أمريكية (القير والمكينة) وتتجمّع بالصين؟
- لا، مو قطع أمريكية مستوردة. المكينة والقير الاثنين يُصنّعان داخل الصين بترخيص/تصميم فورد.

المكينة جديدة ولا موجودة سابقاً عند فورد بأمريكا؟

Its a nice car, but I think they hastened the release and the car has quite a few issues, albeit mostly software which I hope can be resolved.  I've had the car for 3 weeks now and my observations are,
1. Too many glitches in the software including carplay connection issues, the screen freezes or skips too often to enjoy the car.  Its like it can't handle to many things going at the same time, its very frustrating.  I hope this is not a hardware issue.  
2. Too many driving alarms that you can't turn off, so you won't have a quiet ride to enjoy on the highway or in tight spaces. 
3. Radio reception is really bad, hardly anything sounding crisp. 
4. Does not show outside temp. 
5. Does not read the road speed signs
6. Adaptive cruise control is very jerky
7. On two road trips and starting with 100% charge (not 80%) and a full tank at 125km/h cruising speed, I was only able to get 700km range at best. 
8. Due to its boxy design the car really uses a lot of KW at higher cruising speeds, the difference in KW usage between 100km/h and 125km/h is almost double (24kw vs 40kw) so to get the 900+ range they claim, you will need to drive at only 100km/h cruising speed.   
9. The generator can get noisy when the battery is running out, so you will definitely notice it.  Yes the generator is a small 1.5T, but it gets really thirsty when it needs to charge the battery while cruising. 
10. Car came with no carpets, dealer says will be provided later with no ETA. 
11. iCaur accessories not available yet, no ETA. 
12. The panaromic is nice, but peak afternoon I feel the sun on my head and wish I can cover it.  
13. Phone app has some glitches, E.g. does not show accurate tire pressure etc. 
14. Sometimes the car stays ON even though the key is very far away, so you will have to manually lock it every time to know for certain it's OFF. 
15. The front window catches a load of bugs due to the upright angle.  
16. Front seats are ok, but not for long trips. 

The dealer says a software update is on the way but with no ETA which is frustrating.  It is a nice car, and this is my second chinese car, its like they can get 95% of everything right and they don't have time for the final 5% in fine tuning everything and need to pump new models as quick as possible.

Fun fact, technically when going 503kmph the outsides of the tires are actually constantly switching between 1006 kmph (at the top) and 0 kmph (at the bottom)

Wheel speed is typically calculated based on input from an abs sensor and slotted ring on the wheel hubs, but in this instance it is GPS.

With items that are rotating you are typically interested in angular momentum, not linear momentum.

Either way, this is completely untrue. The only point in the wheel that is seeing nearly 0kmph would be the absolute center of the wheel.

To have the car going at 503kmph, the point on the tire that touches the ground at any particular instant has to travel at the exact same speed in the opposite direction.

You talked about angular velocity, which doesn't play any sort of a significant role in this case, as the radius of the wheel is constant, which makes the linear velocity the decisive factor. So if the ongoing wear and the shearing stress on the tire is neglected, the speed of the said point (the one in contact with the ground at any particular time) will turn out to be 503kmph in the opposite direction (linear velocity = Angular velocity * Radius).

[USER] From Gemini: "A serial production car (also called a series production or standard production car) is a vehicle manufactured in a standardized, repeatable assembly process for the general public market.

Key Characteristics

• Not a Prototype or Concept: The car has passed all design, testing, validation, and regulatory approval stages (often marked by the Start of Production or SOP milestone).
• Identical or Batch-Built Units: Instead of a unique, hand-built vehicle or a one-off custom build, serial production cars are made on an assembly line with interchangeable, identical parts.
• Lifecycle Timing: A car enters serial production when its model year rolls out for sale and remains in serial production until the manufacturer discontinues or redesigns the model."

In my own words, essentially it means that they are making many of them and they are all mostly the same, anyone can buy one (if you have the money), and it' street legal. The figures you mentioned (523 HP and 0-100 km/h in 4.5 seconds) are the exact same performance specs as the 2026 BYD Sealion 7 Excellence AWD. Here is why the numbers and years might look different online:

Horsepower Translation: The "523 HP" figure is simply the Imperial/US measurement (BHP). This is the exact mathematical equivalent to the "530 PS" (metric horsepower) rating used in the European market for the 390 kW dual-motor setup.

Model Year Marketing: Calling it a "2027" model is purely a marketing practice. In the global automotive industry, cars released, delivered, or reviewed late in the year are often labeled with the upcoming year as their "Model Year" (MY27) by overseas dealerships and media.

Underneath the naming conventions, both the 2026 and "2027" models share the exact same hardware and software:

The e-Platform 3.0 Evo with the 91.3 kWh Blade (LFP) CTB battery.

The 8-in-1 drive unit and identical dual-motor AWD system.

The Qualcomm Snapdragon 8155 processor and Dynaudio sound system in the cabin.

The same operating system receiving identical Over-The-Air (OTA) updates.

Whether an article or video calls it a 2026 or a 2027, it is the identical vehicle.

The Shark has independent electric motors in each axle. They heavily rely on break based torque vectoring. When one wheel in one axle loses traction, all the power goes to be wasted on that wheel. The car will try to use the calipers to break the free spinning wheel in order to send the power to the other wheel which has traction. But it's not very effective since it's really difficult for the software to adjust perfectly at the right moment.

The Shark has a new mode called Rage mode that limits slipping to the maximum and will engage the breaks hard and almost immediately.
However, in a situation like this one where you'd want to have both wheels in an axle spinning together in low traction conditions, it's just not going to work. It's still an open diff in the end. Power just can't be split, only sent to one wheel in low traction conditions.

Oh, and the reason why they dug so deep is because of the instant torque of the electric motors. It's great for grippy surfaces because you get that instant response, but really bad for mud and sand because the tires just get buried immediately.

It's full-time AWD — not traditional 4WD. BYD's DMO system uses two independent electric motors (one per axle), no prop shaft, with full-time electronic torque. No low-range gearbox, but it has terrain modes including Sand.

Strengths for dunes:
• Instant torque (650–700 Nm) – great for loose sand 
 • 230mm ground clearance, decent approach/departure angles
• Sand mode optimizes traction and throttle response

Limitations:
 • No 4L (low-range) — relies purely on electric motor torque for steep climbs
 •No mechanical locking diffs
 • Heat buildup can cause power throttling during extreme/extended dune bashing. Runs best with a charged battery
• Good for moderate dunes, desert road trips, and casual dune bashing — comfortable and torquey.

Not a replacement for a Land Cruiser 70 or Nissan Patrol for extreme Liwa-style dunes. Think lifestyle adventure ute, not a hardcore desert crawler.

China's electric vehicle (EV) policy is a derivative of its broader energy policy. China initially promoted New Energy Vehicles (NEVs) to tackle strategic energy vulnerabilities, specifically its heavy reliance on imported oil, alongside severe urban air pollution. Over time, the sector evolved into a pillar of industrial and climate policy to hit national carbon-neutrality targets.

Energy Security and Independence
- Oil vulnerability: China lacks sufficient domestic oil reserves to match its rapid rise in car ownership, making oil imports a key national security risk.
- Electrifying transport: Shifting mobility away from internal combustion engines directly curtails future demand for imported petroleum.

Environmental and Climate Goals
- Urban pollution: Early pushes sought to clean up smog-heavy cities by reducing tailpipe emissions.
- Carbon targets: The push aligns with China's formal goals to peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.

Industrial Strategy and Integration
- Supply chain dominance: Energy transition goals merged with state industrial planning to dominate battery and critical mineral supply chains.
- Grid and efficiency standards: Policies tie vehicle manufacturing directly to energy metrics, such as strict national electricity consumption limits enforced on passenger EVs.

The success of China's EV industry is just the tip of the iceberg. Western media fails to see the big picture. The real success story is China's accelerated shift toward energy independece.

As someone who’s spent 20 years in the automotive industry across Detroit and Stuttgart, watching this breakdown of BYD’s production is both sobering and fascinating. We in the West really need to stop dismissing them as 'just another Chinese brand.' Here are a few things that hit home for us professionals:

Vertical Integration is the New King: While we’re stuck negotiating with Tier-1 suppliers for every chip and sensor, BYD is building their own world. Their FinDreams Powertrain subsidiary is doing what GM and Ford dreamt of doing decades ago. It gives them an unbeatable lead in speed-to-market.

The Death of the 'Legacy Hybrid' Logic: Toyota perfected the parallel hybrid (engine-first), but BYD’s DM-i 'Electric-First' architecture is arguably more suited for the 2020s. Using the ICE primarily as a range extender at its peak thermal efficiency (43%!) is a massive engineering win that we haven't quite scaled yet.

The Manufacturing Pace Gap: 97% automation? A car every 60 seconds? That’s Giga-Press level efficiency but applied across the entire hybrid lineup. Our legacy assembly lines look prehistoric in comparison.

Cost Advantage: Because they own the lithium mines AND the battery tech (the Blade Battery), they’ve solved the biggest cost barrier for PHEVs. We are struggling to keep MSRPs under $40k for decent hybrids, while they are dominating the $15k-$25k bracket globally.

Honestly, if the West doesn’t ramp up its R&D and move away from slow-moving supply chains, we aren’t just looking at competition; we’re looking at a complete paradigm shift. BYD isn't just catching up—they’ve changed the rules of the game.
